o: Maintain text with a cursor supporting insert, backspace of up to k chars, and cursor moves, returning up to 10 chars left of the cursor after moves. Since k ≤ 40 and calls ≤ 2e4, an O(k)-per-operation structure suffices. The classic trick: split the text at the cursor into a left stack and a right stack; the cursor sits between them. Example trace: after addText("leetcode") the left stack holds "leetcode"; deleteText(4) pops 4 chars leaving "leet"; etc.
k: Two stacks (left of cursor, right of cursor) give O(1) amortized insert/delete/move.
Moving left pops from left-pushes to right; moving right is the reverse.
The last min(10,len) chars left of the cursor are simply the top 10 entries of the left stack.

a.i: addText pushes onto the left stack; deleteText pops up to k; cursorLeft transfers up to k chars left→right; cursorRight transfers right→left (order preserved automatically because stacks reverse twice). Queries read the top of the left stack.
s: Keep arrays l (chars left of cursor, end = cursor) and r (chars right of cursor, start = cursor).
addText: push each char to l.
deleteText(k): pop up to k from l, return count.
cursorLeft/cursorRight: transfer up to k chars between stacks; return join of last min(10, |l|) chars of l.
a.t: O(k) per operation — each moved/deleted/added character is handled once; queries are O(10).
a.sp: O(total text length) across the two stacks.

w: This is the intended O(k) follow-up solution; alternatives include a doubly linked list with a tail pointer or a gap buffer. Pitfall: returning the preview in the correct order (stack tops are the characters nearest the cursor, so build the string accordingly — in Java, prepending via insert(0,...)). Edge cases: deleting/moving more than available silently clamps, and cursorRight when the right stack is empty returns whatever remains. Follow-up: support arbitrary-length jumps efficiently with a balanced BST / rope keyed by position.
